title: Money: pounds and pence that add up

terminal.description: A shell in your workspace. Run the till here, and try your classes from main.

tasks.title: Add up the till
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 1`, write a class `Till` with two methods. `static BigDecimal total(List<String> prices)` gives back the prices added up, each price written as text such as `"3.35"`, and 0 for an empty list. `static boolean sameAmount(BigDecimal a, BigDecimal b)` says whether `a` and `b` are the same amount of money, so `2.0` and `2.00` are the same.

Check hands `total` lists of prices of its own, some of which a `double` adds up wrong, and compares what comes back with the right total by its value, so `8.00` and `8.0` both count. It hands `sameAmount` pairs with the same amount written with different numbers of decimal places, and pairs that differ.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson about why a double drifts and how a BigDecimal is made.
Write total: start from zero, and add a BigDecimal made from each price's text.
Write sameAmount, and read the part of the lesson about comparing amounts first.
Take the // off the first lines of main and run the file.
hints: A double holds 0.10 only nearly, so do not let a price become a double on its way, not even for a moment. The text of a price is exact.

A BigDecimal made from text holds exactly what the text says. Adding one to another gives back a new BigDecimal and leaves both as they were, as a String's methods do. equals also compares how many decimal places each has.
`sum = sum.add(new BigDecimal(price));` inside a loop over `prices`, starting from `BigDecimal.ZERO`. For sameAmount: `return a.compareTo(b) == 0;`.

tasks.title: Price a group and share a bill
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 2`, write a class `Pricing` with two methods. `static BigDecimal groupFare(BigDecimal adult, int people)` gives back the adult fare times `people`, less 15 percent (times `0.85`), rounded once, at the end, to two decimal places, a half penny up. `static BigDecimal share(BigDecimal total, int people)` gives back what each person pays: `total` divided by `people`, to two decimal places, a half penny up.

Check calls both with amounts of its own, chosen so that a `double` on the way, rounding the wrong way at a half penny, and rounding before the end each give another answer. It compares what comes back with `equals`, so the two decimal places count: `3.3` is not `3.30`.
nextSteps: Read the parts of the lesson about rounding and about dividing.
Write groupFare: multiply first, and round once, on the whole amount.
Write share: tell divide how many decimal places to keep and how to round.
Try both from main, and try 10.00 shared by 3 with a divide that has nothing more.
hints: Rounding the fare of one person and then multiplying adds up the pennies rounded off. And 0.85 is a price-like number too: where it comes from matters as much as where the prices come from.

A BigDecimal can be set to a number of decimal places, and is told how to round when it has to. Of the ways to round, one sends a half penny up and everything under it down. A division that never ends needs the same two answers.

tasks.title: Print an amount, and read one back
tasks.description:
Under `// Task 3`, write a class `Printer` with two methods. `static String ticketLine(BigDecimal amount)` gives back the amount as the ticket shows it: a pound sign, then the amount with exactly two decimal places, a half penny up, and a point between pounds and pence, as in `£1.70`. `static BigDecimal readAmount(String text)` gives back the amount a text such as `" £3.35 "` says, with the spaces at either end and the pound sign left off. When the rest is not an amount, it throws an `IllegalArgumentException` whose message names the text, with the first exception as its cause.

Check calls `ticketLine` with amounts of its own and reads the text letter by letter. It runs with the language of a computer in Germany, where numbers are written with a comma, so a ticket that follows the computer's language shows. It hands `readAmount` amounts and texts that are not amounts, compares an amount by its value, and reads an exception by its type, whether its message names the text, and its cause.
nextSteps: Read the part of the lesson about writing an amount out, and the part about a bad amount.
Write ticketLine: two decimal places first, then the text.
Write readAmount: take off the spaces, then the pound sign, then read the rest.
Catch what reading a bad amount throws, and throw what the task asks for in its place.
hints: An amount written out as it is keeps the decimal places it has, and an amount written by String.format follows the language of the computer it runs on.

Set the scale before you write the amount out. A BigDecimal's own text never depends on the computer. For readAmount, part 5 took the spaces off the ends of a text, and showed how to catch one exception and throw another with it as the cause.

`return "£" + amount.setScale(2, RoundingMode.HALF_UP).toPlainString();`. In readAmount, `trim()`, then `substring(1)` when it starts with `"£"`, then `new BigDecimal(rest)` in a try, and `throw new IllegalArgumentException("Not an amount: " + text, e);` in its catch.
